transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well… it sounds silly when I say it out loud, but it’s spiders, really. I keep arranging my whole house around not having to see them. Like, I’ll put off doing laundry because it’s in the basement, and the basement is… you know, where they tend to be. And the garden shed too—I used to keep everything organized in there, actually, I’m a teacher so I’m normally quite on top of things, labels and all that—but now I avoid going in.

I’ve even started paying people to do little jobs I know I could do myself, just because I can’t make myself go into those spaces. It’s embarrassing, but it’s gotten to the point where it’s affecting ordinary things at home.
When you think about spiders, do you feel afraid?

Yes—very afraid. I mean, I know logically that a spider in the corner of an old house probably isn’t going to hurt me. I teach teenagers, for heaven’s sake, I can be perfectly rational about lots of things. But the moment I picture one dropping out of a box or sitting near the washer, it just… it feels enormous and threatening. Much more than it should. It’s embarrassing to admit.
When you see a spider, do you suddenly get strong physical symptoms like your heart racing or feeling short of breath?

Yes, it comes on immediately. If I actually see one, my chest sort of tightens right away, and my hands start shaking. It’s odd because I can be standing there thinking, “Don’t be ridiculous,” but my body’s already gone ahead of me.

Sometimes I just freeze in the doorway, and other times I’m backing out so fast I’ve barely registered doing it. Like with the basement steps—well, I keep meaning to repaint those, actually—but if there’s a spider there, I’m just gone.
